summary_paragraph: A 60-year-old woman with a history of coronary artery disease s/p CABG and stents, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia was admitted for sudden-onset substernal chest pain and ST elevations on EKG, concerning for STEMI. Cardiac catheterization revealed no new obstructive lesions, suggesting an aborted myocardial infarction. She was managed medically with dual antiplatelet therapy and adjustment of beta-blocker for hypertension. During admission, her elevated creatinine (1.4–1.5 mg/dL) was attributed to acute tubular necrosis, likely from recent dehydration. Her poorly controlled diabetes (A1c 12.5%) prompted an increase in Lantus insulin from 50 to 65 units daily, with transition to an insulin pen for ease of use. An infected epidermal cyst on her back was incised and drained, with culture growing Staphylococcus aureus, treated with doxycycline. Prurigo nodules from chronic scratching were managed with triamcinolone cream. Social work addressed her non-adherence and lack of support, recommending evaluation for long-term assisted care. She was discharged home with services and follow-up arranged.
problems: Coronary atherosclerosis of native coronary artery
Acute kidney failure with lesion of tubular necrosis
Diabetes mellitus without mention of complication, type II or unspecified type, not stated as uncontrolled
